maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-POWERS OF RAILWAY COMMISSION.
RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-POWERS OF RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
NORTHRUP (E. Hastings) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 39) to amend the Railway Act. He said: Last session the government introduced a Bill to amend the Railway Act so as to confer certain additional powers on the Board of Railway Commissioners, giving the Board jurisdiction in complaints made by the Crown or by a corporation with regard to certain specified matters. The list included a number of matters on the face of it, but mainly matters with regard to which negotiations are not usually conducted as contracts made between a corporation or the Crown and the railways. I propose to add to, along the same line, that the commissioners should have power in contracts made with regard to the operation of the road. It is well known that contracts are made between municipalities and the government or a railway company, and that in the overwhelming majority of cases, they refer to the operation of the road. In consideration of the operation of the road, a bonus is given by the municipality or a subsidy granted by parliament. Exactly in the line with the government measure of last year, I propose to give the commissioners authority with regard to such contracts.
In one other respect this Bill goes further than the amendment of last session. Under that law, appeals of the kind to which I have referred can only be made in cases between the Crown or corporation and the railway with which the contract was made. It is well known that, in this country, there are practically only two or three railways. In the great majority of cases contracts are made between the Crown or a corporation and some minor railway which has been subsidized for a part of the country through
which it runs; and, usually, after the contract is made and the railway constructed, this minor railway is absorbed by one of the larger railway corporations. The result is that the larger railway has the benefit of the money which the municipality or Crown has expended, while the municipality or the Crown loses the benefit of the contract on account of which alone the money was advanced. The Bill which I have now the honour to propose would aiiow the board t, >
act in such a case, and would provide that the railway which has_ possession of the property in consideration of which the bonus is given should be held responsible for carrying out the contract made by the road which has been absorbed and which, having gone out of operation, cannot be held to its contract. This, it will be seen, is on the same line as the government Bill of last session, but it extends the principle a little further in the two directions I have indicated.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

That in the opinion of the House it is advisable to appoint a Select Standing Committee of the House to deal with questions relating to Marine and Fisheries as they arise from time to time, and that the rules of the House be amended accordingly.
He said:	Mr. Speaker; during the last
session of this House I had the honour to ihove a resolution similar in its terms to the one I now propose, and while no opposition was offered, yet no action was taken to carry its purpose into effect. Of course, you will recollect that the government were so very much engaged during the last session, and the opposition were so very busy trying to get into power that my resolution necessarily did not receive that attention which its importance deserved. I trust, Sir, that I will have better luck this time and that some action will be taken by parliament to give effect to my proposal. I was very much interested' in the speech of the leader of the opposition delivered in the ^House last Monday in favour of conserving our natural resources. That speech contained a great deal of valuable and useful information, and we will of course all agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) as to the vital necessity of conserving the natural resources of Canada. However, in the motion which I now place before the House I am not thinking so much about conserving natural resources as I am advocating the development of a great Canadian industry which has enormous possibilities for adding to the wealth and prosperity of our land. My idea is that it would be a great improvement over existing conditions if we should have a special Marine and Fisheries committee meeting year after year and devoting its labour an'd research, to the development of the fishing industry of this country. There seems to be a growing tendency amongst all legislative bodies to relegate the general work of legislation to special committees which have opportunities for ascertaining the facts, considering them, tabulating them, and placing them before parliament so that parliament may consider the results, and take whatever action is needed, or that may be recommended. For example, 100 years ago there were only five select standing committees in the Congress of the United States, but as the country became larger, as new states were added, and as new interests arose the committees of Congress increased until during last session there were no fewer than 50 committees considering different questions.
They have such committees as that on elections, ways and means, appropriations, judiciary, banking and currency, coin and weights and measures, commerce, rivers Mr. FOSTER.
and harbours, the merchant marine and fisheries. Thirteen members constitute this latter committee of congress which deals with all questions relating to . the merchant marine and the fisheries. It was made a standing committee on December 21, 1887. They have also committees on agriculture, foreign affairs, military affairs, naval affairs, the post office and post roads, public lands, Indian affairs, territories, railways and canals, manufactures, mines and mining, public buildings and grounds, Pacific railroads, improvement of the Mississippi river, education, labour, militia, patents and so on, 50 committees in all to do the work of congress, which is apportioned to these various committees and tabulated and made ready for consideration by the House. In the Canadian parliament, as you are aware, we have ten select standing committees of this House, the committees on agriculture and colonization, banking and commerce, railways, public accounts and so on, all doing useful work. In Great Britain there is a committee on trade which under the rules of the imperial parliament, deals with questions relating to marine and fisheries. In the province of Nova Scotia, for 50 years prior to confederation, there was a select standing committee of the legislature of that province for the consideration of questions relating to the fisheries. This was also true, I believe, of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, I am not familiar with the practice of the other provinces. At the time of confederation, when all questions relating to the fisheries were handed over to the federal parliament, these committees were discontinued in these local legislatures and it is rather a remarkable circumstance that we have allowed fifty years of confederation to pass away without a select standing committee of this House to deal with questions relating to marine affairs or to our fisheries.
In raising this question last year I gave the House considerable information that I had collected showing the great importance of our fishing industry. I pointed out our immense coast line on the eastern shore of Canada being about 6,000 miles in length. Then we have also, a very prolific fishing district on the western coast, and including the northern waters we have about 15,000 miles of coast line in this country. We have a great many people engaged in this great industry. In the province of Nova Scotia alone there are 25,000 men engaged in it. If you multiply that number by five, to include their families, you have about 125,000 persons, about one quarter of the whole population of our province directly dependent on the fishing industry. Taking all of the provinces of Canada we have about 76,000 men on our coasts making a living on the sea in this

way. If you include the men and boys .gnd girls engaged in packing, there are about 88,000 in all, showing that a very large proportion of the population of Canada are engaged in this industry. A very large amount of capital is invested in the industry and the output each year amounts to something in the vicinity of thirty million dollars. The industry is only in its infancy. It is capable of great development. The two great requisites for the development of this industry are better transportation facilities and a better market.
The source of supply, the ocean, is inexhaustible; it is simply a question of putting the fish on the market in a proper way.
The present administration have done a great deal in that direction for which they should receive credit. They have provided a system of cold storage for bait which has done a great deal in Nova Scotia to assist the fishing industry. In former years it was very difficult in the spring to find bait for the fishing vessels. The bait visits the coast in the fall of the year and disappear in a few weeks. But by the present system it is preserved until the spring when it is ready for use and in that way the ships and fishing boats are able to fit out and go to sea and to work in the early part of the season which they could not do formerly. Then the present administration have done a great deal in the way of the propagation of fish along the coast, the propagation of lobsters for example, which is one of the most important branches of the industry. They have also given us better transportation facilities, they have given us an increased number of refrigerator cars and have placed a daily fast freight between Halifax and Mulgrave and Montreal. The train of course does not reach Montreal in a day but it leaves daily, it has a schedule time and we know it will arrive there in reasonable time. The express rate per hundred for carrying fish from Halifax or Mulgrave to Montreal has by this arrangement been reduced from $1.50 to 38 cents which has done a great deal to stimulate the industry in that direction. Then the government has done something in the way of subsidizing steamers to collect fish at points where the Intercolonial Railway touches the sea, which is also very important and at those points where the steamers have called the trade has expanded in much greater ratio than at other points where they have not these facilities. I believe that a great deal more can be profitably done in that direction. An expansion of this system would not only furnish business for the Intercolonial Railway but also develop this important industry along the coast. Then we have also had, as you know, a number of break-16i
waters and wharfs constructed along the shores of the maritime provinces all of which have been useful in the development of this great industry. The coast has been well lighted and buoyed during the last few years. All of these things are assisting but a great deal remains to be done. I am glad to see that the Department of Trade and Commerce has taken this matter up and shown some interest in it. I am also glad that the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is showing an interest in this great question and that the government are continuing the good work they commenced some years ago. I submit that there is a great deal of work for this committee to do, and I feel sure that there will be no opposition to it on either side of the House. I shall therefore not take up more of your time but shall move the resolution which is in your hands.

Representing, as I do, a constituency the people of which are largely interested in the fishing industry, I cannot refrain from making a few observations with regard to .this resolution. There is an impression throughout the country, I think I may go further and say there is a belief throughout the country, that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is in need of the services of a surgeon. I do not know how deeply that belief has penetrated this House, but the hon. gentleman who has moved this resolution, instead of suggesting the bringing in of a surgeon, has advised calling in a standing committee. Well, Mr. Speaker, standing committees are no doubt of great value. For instance we have a standing committee of this House on agriculture which has done excellent service, but the value of which is not perhaps always recognized, because notwithstanding the fact that the Standing Committee on Agriculture has done excellent work, we find that the different governments of the day have, each in its turn, from time immemorial, claimed all the credit for abundant harvests and leaving Divine Providence, the farmers and the Standing Committee on Agriculture out in the cold. My hon. friend who has moved this resolution, has made, it seems to me, a very excellent case for some change in the administration of the Atlantic fisheries. There can be no doubt that those fisheries are of the utmost value and capable of great development, but it is equally undoubted that they are not to-day in that flourishing condition they ought to enjoy and which, with better methods of administration, they would experience. I have no desire to occupy much of the time of the House, but I think it well, at this particular stage, to draw attention to the decrease in the number of those permanently employed in the Atlantic fisheries during the past quarter of a century. In doing this I

take, as the basis of my computation the number of persons to whom the bounty has been paid out of the funds set aside by the Dominion government for that purpose. It seems to me that such is the only true test to be applied in order to arrive at the actual number of those constantly engaged in that industry; and I find that these figures fall very much below these given in the Year-book from time to time.
In the year 1882 the total number of fishermen drawing bounties was 29,932. In Nova Scotia the number was 17,473. Eight years later-and I may say that I have divided the quarter of a century into three periods-in 1890 the number had increased to 39,050, being an increase of 9,118. In that year there were 20,673 fishermen employed in Nova Scotia who drew bounty, being an increase in that province alone of 3,200. In 1898 the number had fallen to 29,402, a decrease of 9,648; and in the province of Nova Scotia the number fell to 17,278, or a decrease, in that province alone, of no less than 3,395. In 1907 there was a further decrease. The total then stood at 25,920, showing a falling off of 3,482, while in Nova Scotia it stood at 13,917, or a decrease of 3,361. In other words, in less than 17 years, the total decrease in the number of drawing this fishing bounty was no less than 13,130, and in Nova Scotia alone no less than 6,756.
Has my hon. friend the figures showing the catch of fish in those years?

I have not the figures under my hand, nor do I think it possible to secure figures giving accurately the catch of fish in any statistical work published by the department. A great deal of what would be valuable statistical matter, if accurate, is obtained by the department from year 'to year, but I fear that in this connection very little importance can be attached to those statistics because they are _not altogether reliable. The same condition prevailed in Great Britain a few years ago, and when it was brought to the attention of the particular board or department having charge of such matters, the suggestion was at first scoffed at that anything could be wrong in connection with the statistics published; but a most careful and complete investigation showed that these figures, published from year to year, were absolutely without value, and, upon the best information which I can obtain, the statistics regarding our Atlantic fisheries are to-day utterly valueless as giving any accurate idea of the total catch of fish or its market value. Let me point out one instance in which these returns are untrustworthy. A certain quantity of fish is caught and later on the fish is dried and exported as dry fish. The fishery officer comes along and asks each fisherman how many thousand pounds of green Mr. JAMESON.
fish he has caught, and takes down his reply. Then he goes to the man who cures these fish and asks him how many cured fish he has handled during the year, and this man says so many thousand quintals. The fishery officer then adds the total of green and cured fish together, and thus, in many cases, double the quantity of fish actually caught is included in the total column. I am not saying that any particular blame attaches to the fishery officers or the department. The practice is one which has grown up and which is due more or less to the fact that it has been found very difficult indeed to get reliable information of this character. So that it is high time, if we are to make these statistics of any value to the country, that a careful revision of the work should be undertaken; and no better means for doing that could be found than this committee which my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has suggested. The fact that there has been a decline in the fishing industry of the maritime provinces is one to which I wish to draw particular attention. That they are declining many of our fishermen are ready to admit and at least throughout Nova Scotia, our fishermen have for some time become alive to the fact that some change is necessary, if they are to get the most profit that can be had out of the fisheries. With that obect in view they have associated themselves together at the different fishing stations along the coast into organizations known as Fishermen's Unions. These unions meet together from time to time to discuss everything relating to their interests and frame resolutions. Then, annually or more frequently, delegates from these unions meet and endeavour to harmonize the resolutions which have been passed by the various local committees or unions and transmit them, perhaps I might say for the benefit of the department, at least I can say for the benefit of those concerned. In this connection, I wish to pay a tribute to the gentleman who was instrumental in having these unions organized and who, I was informed almost single-handed, carried through the legislature of Nova Scotia the Act under which they have come into existence. That gentleman is Mr. M. H. Nickerson, a member of the legislative assembly of Nova Scotia, sitting, I think, for the county of Shelburne.
There has been, throughout the province of Nova Scotia, an agitation on the part of many interested in the fisheries in favour of the creation of what is known as a fishery board, after the pattern of the board of that name which exists in Scotland. I am not personally inclined, with the information I have under my hand and with such study as I have been able to give to the work which the Scotch fishery board has carried into effect, to say that I would advise the creation of just such a board at this

moment but it is a fair subject for careful consideration. The conditions in Scotland differ very considerably from those in Canada with respect to the legislative status of the board. In Canada, we have the administration of the fisheries under a department of the government and the department should do practically what the fishery board might be expected to do, with the exception, perhaps, that the Fishery Board of Scotland is composed in part of men appointed to represent the fishermen themselves. That fishery board is composed of seven members, four representing the fishermen, one a legal adviser, one an expert, and the chairman. The chairman is the only one who receives a salary, the others getting only their travelling expenses. The object of the fishery board in Nova Scotia, if created, would be, briefly, to remove, if possible, the administration of the fisheries absolutely from the caldron of party politics. That, I think, is a condition which, gentlemen on both sides of the House will admit, is most desirable. Then, they would endeavour to devise and frame suitable regulations with respect to the fisheries and would see to the proper enforcement of these regulations. They would also establish a standard pack and package in connection with the fisheries. Some of the fish which are put up in Nova Scotia are not of as high quality as they might be, or as are put up in some other countries while some are of the very highest quality. This possibly, is owing to the fact that no standard of cure, or pack, or package, has ever been established- That course would necessarily be along educational lines, which would be most desirable, and could well be carried out through the medium of these fishermen's unions, to which I made passing reference a moment ago. Another object of the fishery board would be to seek wider and more profitable markets for the product of our fisheries. That is something most devoutly to be desired. As it is now, the ordinary fisherman has no market beyond the purely local one; but through the medium of these fishermen's unions some plan might be devised whereby a more cooperative work could be carried out, so that the fishermen would gain greater profit from his labour. And let me tell the hon. members of this House that the fishermen are worthy of the utmost consideration that can be bestowed upon them, and that any assistance that can be rendered them by the administration of the day or through the medium of this standing committee would be no more than they are properly entitled to. They are men who, day after day, and year after year, are obliged to go out, and, at the risk of their lives and property, endeavour to win a livelihood for themselves and their families from the turbulent sea. I know that in my own county there are a large number of men who are
fishing throughout the entire year; and to prosecute the fisheries in the winter season on the rugged and blustery Atlantic coast or in the Bay of Fundy is certainly no child's play. The man who follows such a life needs a hardy frame, strong limbs, and the heart of a lion.
Now, I wish to refer, before closing, to a new feature which has developed in respect to the in-shore fisheries of certain parts of Nova Scotia and more especially within my own knowledge, to those of the western part of the province: that is, the doing away with the old-time sailboat and adopting in its stead the more noisy but more profitable vessel propelled by a gasolene engine. In a speech made in this House a year or two ago, in moving a motion similar to that now before the House, the hon. member for Guysborougli (Mr. Sinclair) said, or quoted from some writer who said, that the initial cost of embarking upon the inshore fisheries was comparatively insignificant, that all that was necessary was a boat, a few nets, or lines and hooks, and a tub of bait. Conditions have changed in the fisheries, as in almost everything else, and to-day, the fishermen who win their livelihood from the sea have to adopt modern methods and bring their appliances strictly up to date. The cost of a staunch and fairly roomy fishing boat now is much greater than it was even four or five years ago, because it must be made strong enough to carry the gasolene engine. Then, the cost of the engine itself is very considerable, and the expense of operating it amounts to from 25 to 50 cents a day. So, hon. gentlemen will see that the fishing which is prosecuted now throughout the entire year, entails a much greater expense to the individual who carries it on than when sailboats only were used. And the advantage, not only to the fishermen themselves, but to the country, is that in .using these boats they can go out even against an adverse wind, and can get off at almost any time of the tide, and in that way many valuable days are saved and the fishermen are enabled to take advantage of the slack tide to* ply their avocation, which they could not always do in the old-time sail boat.
In conclusion, I heartily endorse the motion of the hon. member for Guysborough in favour of the appointment of this committee. Perhaps I have trespassed unduly upon the time of the House in speaking as I have. As a new member, perhaps I am scarcely justified in occupying so much time. My apology for taking up the time of the House is the importance of this matter from the standpoint of the people of the county I represent, and of many other counties in the province of Nova Scotia. I trust it will be the aim of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to unite in an earnest effort to put this industry upon the best possible basis, in order that the fishermen as

491
individuals, and the country generally, may benefit and prosper thereby.

I *wish to make a suggestion in connection with this motion. We have a good many committees in this House, and the members of those committees have a good deal to do. I think the moving of this resolution is a proper time to bring to the attention of the government and the House the need of a better distribution of the work between this House and the Senate. I believe the time has come when the Senate of Canada ought to be reorganized and be put in a position to take up some of the work that this House now has to perform. If that were done, instead of the Senate now being off on a holiday for a month, they would be discussing fishery questions, they would take up the question of the conservation of the natural resources of this country, they would take up the bankruptcy matter, which was before them some years ago, and which they handled very well. While I have every sympathy with this motion, and would like to see a committee of this House appointed to deal with the question involved, I desire also to say that this House, and perhaps the other House-because I believe they are ready to consider the question as a co-ordinate branch of parliament-should unite in a reorganization, so that the Senate may take up some of these great public questions and deal with them, and thus relieve this House of some of the work it has now to undertake. This House has at present a great deal to do, probably it has more than we can do, and do it as well as it ought to be done. So I take occasion to suggest to the government, not only the consideration of this motion, but the consideration of some plan by which the work would be distributed between the two Houses to the advantage of the performance of public business.

The motion introduced by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is one of great [DOT]interest to me as a member from the maritime provinces. The question he has discussed whether we shall have a standing committee of this House to deal with questions relating to Marine and Fisheries. The arguments advanced by the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) afford a strong reason why we should have such a committee. Such a committee would relieve this House from considerable work and dis-cusion that now devolve upon it in relation to these matters, and would undoubtedly be able to give to them better and more consideration than single members of the House could do. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has suggested an argument for this committee that I had not thought of before, and that was that the Senate had adjourned no doubt to go a fish-Mr. JAMESON.
ing because they had nothing else to do, and if such a committee were formed, some of them might find something to do in connection with it. When you travel along the shores of the province of Nova Scotia- and I am now speaking in the presence of hon. gentlemen who are acquainted with the facts-you will frequently come to a fishing district which, some years ago, was very prosperous, whereas the district is now more or less depleted. You will understand of course that I am now speaking of the shore fisheries. You would probably find some empty houses in the district, whose former occupants, the fishermen, have gone to town or somewhere else. When you go through an interior county and find a farmhouse without a tenant, you make up your mind that the farmer has gone somewhere else, and that the soil is not being tilled. So it is with the shore fishermen. I do not blame this on the government, but I do say, as the hon. member for Guysborough has said, that it is time we had a committee of this House to which matters of that kind might be referred. I have no desire to disparage the manner in which the fisheries are administered by the Marine and Fisheries Department, I do not mean to say that anything has been left undone by the department that should have been done, because I presume they are doing all they possibly can. Nevertheless, our shore fisheries are becoming less every year, and I could say a great many things in relation to that question which might perhaps not be pertinent to the motion before the House. Now my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) said that a fisheries board was required. I think every hon. member of this House has received some resolutions or a report of some gentlemen in the east who are interested in the fishing industry, and who wish to form a fisheries board. I think this also is a matter that could well be referred to such a committee as has been suggested. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the fishing industry generally of Nova Scotia is less prosperous than it has been, but the shore fisheries have certainly become almost a thing of the past, but I may say especially with regard to that good old county of Lunenburg, that were it not for the deep sea fisheries that have been carried on and developed by the good people of that county, our Nova Scotia fisheries generally would not make as good a showing as they do make to-day. Any one who is acquainted with the shore fisheries and with the deep sea fisheries, and can make a distinction between them, will recognize that while the fisheries generally have increased greatly during the last twenty or twenty-five years, the increase in our deep sea fisheries has been very good, but not what it should have been. I do not mean to say that last year was better

than the previous year, because variations are sometimes caused, not only by the condition of the fisheries, but by the way the returns are made, and the lack of good luck that happens to deep sea fishermen. Our deep sea fisheries have increased by leaps and bounds in the last twenty-five years ; but our shore fisheries-and by shore fisheries I mean those which are worked within the three mile limit by what we call boat fishermen-that industry 1 am sorry to say has decreased in Nova Scotia, and that is an industry that we should strive in every way to revive and develop. We talk about our great valuable lands in the west, and we are proud of them. We talk about the development of these lands, and we are proud of it, and are determined to do everything we can to promote that development. But even if you were to do nothing with those lands and let them lie uncultivated, they would still be' there just the same. But if you fail to help and assist the shore fishermen, if you allow the shore fisheries to die out, it will be very difficult indeed to re-establish them in the position we have seen them occupy. I think therefore that the appointment of such a committee as is proposed will be a step in the right direction The cold storage matter has also been referred to, and I congratulate the government on having carried on the cold storage system. But a great deal yet remains to be done, that system is not yet doing all we expected it to do, it is not giving all the accommodation that the government no doubt expected it would give. Now one of the ways by which we can help that system is to appoint a committee who will consider matters relating to cold storage. Cold storage is intended to provide bait for the shore fishermen as well as for the deep sea fishermen. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that any further argument is required to show why such a committee should be appointed, after we have heard the strong arguments advanced by the hon. member for Guysborough. I think this House should have no hesitation in appointing such a committee and I am sure that this industry, which is of very great importance to us and of paramount importance to the Dominion of Canada, will be benefited by the appointment of this committee. This resolution takes a long step in the right direction and I trust this House will have no hesitation in passing the resolution of my hon. friend from Guysborough.

Mr. Speaker, when a resolution similar to the one now on the Order Paper was discussed last year it met, if I remember correctly, with favour from my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and, I think, from my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), as
well as others. I think that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and his followers also concurred in the resolution. Unfortunately, however, it evoked some lengthy discussion, which, I think, occurred on a Wednesday sitting. When six o'clock arrived some hon. member was on his feet discussing the resolution and he unfortunately moved the adjournment of the debate which placed the resolution at the foot of public orders and it was never reached again during the session. I am very glad that the remarks made by all the other speakers to-day have been very brief and to the point, and I desire to say that my observations will not unnecessarily prolong the debate as I would like very much to see this resolution carried before six o'clock. Before giving a few reasons why I think this committee should be appointed, I wish to say that my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), presented some statistics which J think were intended to give to the House the idea that because there were in recerit years a lesser number of applicants for fishing bounties in the province of Nova Scotia there was a reduction in the total value of the fish taken in these waters. I do not think that is correct. I do not wish to provoke any discussion upon the value of our statistics, but I want to say to my hon. friend that in recent years the statistics regarding the number of applicants for fishing bounties have been far more reliable than they were in the years to which my hon. friend referred. The fishing industry is doubtless a great asset. I think that even we who come from the maritime provinces are apt to overlook its great value. We are apt to think of the great agricultural resources of the west, of the mineral resources and of the timber resources of our country, but we should remember that we take, I think, according to statistics, fish from the seas to the value of $40,000,000. I agree with the hon. member for Digby that there is a necessity for better statistics relative to our fisheries. If I remember correctly last year the value of the fisheries, according to the blue-book issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, was about $38,000,000. I think these figures considerably underestimate the value of our fisheries. There is this to be remembered concerning our fisheries: While we are taking annually fish to this great amount from the seas, exporting them to foreign countries and bringing back to Canada coin or some other valuable returns, we are not necessarily depleting our fisheries. We all know that the constant production of crops from the soil lessens its value and productivity and that if we cut down our timber resources it takes considerable time for the timber to reproduce itself. Without any expense on the part of the government our fishermen can go to the waters surrounding this country and take from them fish to a

*very considerable value which adds very much to the national wealth. I wish to give just a few reasons why I think this committee should be appointed and I just wish to refer to four or five matters which I think this committee should deal with. If the committee is appointed I have not the slightest doubt that the work which it will do will be proof of the wisdom of its appointment. A year or two ago I discussed the treaty of 1818 between Great Britain and the United States of America which related principally to the north Atlantic fisheries. On that occasion I took particular pains to discuss a feature of the treaty of 1885, I think the treaty of Washington, which established what is called the modus vivendi and which permits American fishermen certain rights, which rights are prohibited to them in the treaty of 1818. On that occasion I found that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, a great many of my colleagues from the province of Nova Scotia, and a great many members of the House, were of the opinion that the people of this country did not wish to abrogate the modus vivendi clause of this treaty. I thought it was a great mistake to have ever given these privileges to the United States, and I was always very much surprised that that very eminent statesman, Sir Charles Tup-per, should have consented to these privileges being granted However, they were granted and they have been continued by this government since they came into power in 1896. If I appeared before the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or before any member of the government, or before the Governor in Council, and ask for a revocation of the modus vivendi, I probably would be asked to give reasons for it. [ probably would be asked the question if the people of my province desire the revocation of these privileges. It would be very difficult for me to answer that question. As far as my own county is concerned I could answer that question very quickly in the affirmative, I could say the same concerning many other counties in the province of Nova Scotia, but in some counties there would be some opposition to it. I think it is very important that the government should know what is the opinion of the people of the maritime provinces on this ques tion. We should summon before that committee men competent to) give evidence on this question and have it made a matter of public record. The other day my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) was called to Washington to act in conjunction with a representative of the Newfoundland government to prepare a case for reference to the Hague tribunal during the present year. I have no doubt that the interests of Canada and the interests of the maritime provinces in particular were well safeguarded by the Minister of Justice, but he has very little information which he can Mr. A.'k. MACLEAN.
gather in the Department of Marine and Fisheries concerning this question, and I think that if we had had considerable evidence from people who understand the operation of the modus vivendi clause of this treaty in the blue-book, it might have been very valuable to the Minister of Justice the other day at Washington. Last year we had some legislation regarding the Norwegian coasting trade in Canada. I understand that under some old treaty and under some order in council passed by the Canadian government, Norwegian vessels were per mitted to engage in the coasting trade in Canada. When the resolution came up before the House of Commons last session very few men in this House were in a position to give an intelligent vote upon that measure. It is true there were some gentlemen in the House who had given some attention to it, but it was largely a one-sided expression of opinion that came from them. There was a great deal to say for and against the abrogation of that order in council. Now I say had that committee been in existence last year we might have had some representatives of those who wished to continue this order in council and we could have summoned representatives of those who were opposed to the further continuance of the order in council. In this one respect, such a committee could have done valuable, service for this country and it might have contributed very much to the enlightenment of hon. gentlemen on that measure.	.
We heard the complaint made year after year that our Canadian shipping is decreasing and so it is. It is difficult to see what the remedy for that is, but a remedy there may be, and a committee to which would be specially delegated matters relating to Marine and Fisheries could very properly summon to Ottawa gentlemen who are capable of giving expert opinion in reference to the decay of our shipping interests, and making suggestions which might tend to revive and develop it. Another important question is that with reference to steam trawl fishing. In our Atlantic waters, fishing operations are carried on by steam trawlers which come from France. These steam trawlers ply out of two or three ports and in many of the other fishing ports of France there is considerable opposition to this mode of fishing. In certain parts of Nova Scotia it is a very live issue. I hear many complaints from fishermen in my own county who suffer injury to their nets and trawls by the operation of these French steam trawlers. This is a question which has engaged the attention of the British government for many years and they have appointed one or more commissions, but I suppose like all other questions there are two sides to it. However, it is high time that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should take this

question up for consideration. It would be a very easy matter, if this committee were constituted, to summon persons who are acquainted with this mode of fishing and ascertaining their best judgment as to whether steam trawl fishing is injurious or otherwise. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) spoke of the appointment of a fishery board. No doubt there is a great deal to say in favour of the appointment of such a board, and there is something to be said against it. That also is a question on which this committee might advise the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his officers. There are many gentlemen in Nova Scotia who have given a great deal of attention in recent years to this question, and I am sure they would be glad to come before such a committee and give valuable information. On many occasions this government and preceding governments have appointed commissions to travel through the country in order 'to ascertain the views of the people upon lobster fishery regulations ' and other questions concerning our fishing industry. My experience of these commissions is, that while they visit a great many sections of the country and examine a great many witnesses and present a report to the department, the evidence taken is generally so voluminous that it is not, and indeed cannot be read by members of parliament or by anybody else. I doubt very much if even the officials of the department can afford the time to acquaint themselves with the details of the evidence taken by these commissions. In my opinion a special committee of this House would do better work in connection with many of the questions, do it more expeditiously, and at less cost, and give more practical results. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I express the hope that the committee called for by this resolution shall be appointed, and I doubt if amongst all our select standing committees there can be found one which can do more excellent work than this committee would be capable of doing. I am sure such a committee will prove a very valuable aid to the Minister of Marine, to his department, to the officials, to every member of the House of Commons, and to the country generally.

KYTE (Richmond, N.S.) I desire, Mr. Speaker, to say a word or two by way of supplementing what has been said by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. McLean). I can assure you, Sir, that it is with great interest I have listened to the discussion which has been promoted by the resolution moved by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). In this parliament we are called upon, from time to time, to deal with great questions; questions in which are involved the prosperity and the happiness of our people, but in my opinion no more important question
than the one now under consideration could be submitted to us. I was very much edified by the speech of the hon. gentleman who moved the address in reply to His Excellency's speech at the opening of parliament. I was much pleased that he gave such prominence to the agricultural industry as one of the great sources of our national wealth, nor do I think that the hon. gentleman over-stated the importance of that industry, but, Sir, the vast importance of the fishery industry of Canada must not be forgotten by this parliament. I think I may fairly conclude from the tenor of the speeches of hon. gentlemen that there is no controversy as to the propriety of adopting this motion. I take it for granted that the consensus of opinion is that a committee such as that proposed is a proper insitution to add to the existing organization of the House of Commons, and that being so it is perhaps not necessary for me to prolong the discussion. But, Sir, may I have your permission to make one or two observations with respect to the statement made by the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) to the effect that the fisheries of Nova Scotia are declining. I am not disposed to accept that as a fact. I believe that the changed conditions which undoubtedly do exist in respect to our fisheries are not due at all to their depletion, but rather to change in the methods of prosecuting the industry. We must not forget that many years ago the most remunerative return from the fisheries of the maritime provinces accrued from the salt fish. Forty or fifty years ago there was a large and remunerative market for salt fish, but from year to year that market has dwindled, until to-day the necessity has arisen for the fishermen of the maritime provinces placing the products of their industry upon the markets of the world in the form of fresh fish.
I	believe that there are great opportunities of development in this country that can keep the fishing industry quite apace with all possible demands which may be made upon it by reason of the increased population of the western provinces. The government are each year spending large sums of money to induce immigrants to occupy the fertile plains of the west, and are building railways to afford these people railway accommodation and such means of transportation as will give them the best possible facilities for the handling of the products of their labours. One of the most important of all the duties which this committee would be called upon to discharge would be to consider that very question of transportation. We are face to face with the fact that the fishermen of the maritime provinces are not able to send the products of their industry into the centres of population throughout Canada and as a consequence the fishing industry is not as remu-

nerative for them as it otherwise might he. I do hope that one of the first matters to be taken into consideration by this committee is that very question of transportation, in order to see if we cannot devise some means by which the fresh fish of Nova Scotia can be sent forward to Ontario, Quebec, and the west with that facility with which the manufactured goods and the flour of Ontario and western Canada are sent into the maritime provinces. The interchange of commodities spoken of some thirty or forty years ago as likely to arise from the construction of the Intercolonial Kailway has not taken place with that plenitude that the supporters of confederation at one time hoped for. I am rather inclined to think that the balance of trade has been altogether against the maritime provinces; the people of Ontario and Quebec, enterprising as they are, have got rather the best of us in the matter of trade, and while they have sent down hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of their manufactured products into the maritime provinces they have taken very little from us except the actual money paid for the purchase of their goods.
It is upon the natural resources of the maritime provinces that we must rely to make up that interchange of commodities which should exist between the eastern and western provinces. We do send some coal into Quebec and a very small portion into Ontario, but apart from that item we send scarcely anything into western Canada or into the great central provinces. The question of transportation is the obstacle which has retarded the development of the increase which I have suggested, and I am firmly of the opinion that that condition might be ameliorated if this question of transportation were taken up and the products of the fisheries of the maritime provinces were given a special rate by which they would be able to reach the populous centres of Canada.
I have said that the apparent decline in the fisheries of the maritime provinces is not due to the depletion of that industry but rather to a change of conditions. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) referred to the fact that in western Nova Scotia the sail boat is largely disappearing and the fishermen are resorting to gasolene boats for the prosecution of their industry. I must confess that I am not sufficiently familiar with the customs regulations on that point, but as the time has come when it is absolutely necessary for the fishermen of the maritime provinces to prosecute their calling by gasolene boats rather than by the ordinary sail and row boats, the purchase of these engines is going to amount to a considerable item to the fishermen. The Minister of Customs might then well consider if he cannot find his way clear Mr. KYTE.
to reduce to some extent at least the duty on gasolene engines which will hereafter become an actual necessity for the fishermen of this country.
The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) referred to another question which is of vital importance to the people of the maritime provinces, that of the coasting privileges enjoyed by vessels flying a foreign flag. That question was to some extent settled, I understand, by an order in council passed some six or seven months ago, but there are, it appears to me, other questions involved in that which may well occupy the attention of this House and the appointing of a committee as suggested this afternoon would simplify to my mind a great many of the difficulties that would be encountered were we obliged to present these questions to the full House. I do not imagine for a moment that the people who are engaged in the fishing industry of Canada are less capable of prosecuting their calling than they were in the past. I am convinced that were the opportunities given to them and were the changed conditions which have come about in the last twenty years in relation to that industry, simplified and made easier for them by means of such legislation and such acts of co-operation as this parliament can bring about, the shore fisheries of the maritime provinces would be as profitable as ever they were.
To illustrate this point, let me say that in the last season the fishermen of the maritime provinces, or of Nova Scotia at all events, enjoyed the satisfaction of getting the greatest amount of shore fish that they have taken in any season during the last forty years.	The catch of mackerel in
Nova Scotia far exceeded that of any other year and naturally we would be inclined to the opinion that last year was a most profitable year for the fishermen. I regret, however, to have to say that the very contrary was the case. The fishermen of Nova Scotia, not having markets or means of transportation available which would enable them to send their fish fresh into 'such markets as purchase fish in that condition, lost a large proportion of their catch by reason of being unable to cure them; and when they cured them they lost a great proportion of their profit by reason of the falling market resulting from the large catch in eastern Nova Scotia. Thus we come back to the great question of transportation, which after all is the one affecting the price of fish to our people and I would be glad indeed if this committee, if appointed, would take into consideration that question, which transcends, I believe, all others affecting the prosperity of our fishing population.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing as I

do a very large body of fishermen in the maritime provinces, and as almost all of the members of this House who represent fishing counties have spoken, it would probably be regarded as indifference on my part if I allowed this opportunity to pass without saying something on behalf of the large body of fishermen in my county. At the outset, let me congratulate the hon. gentlemen who are new members in this House, like myself, who have spoken on this question, particularly the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) who has just taken his seat, upon the very excellent presentation of his case and of his own abilities as a representative which he has made in this House. The same would apply to my hon. friends, the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) and the member for Digby (Mr. Jameson). The only little cloud upon the horizon in the remarks of my hon. friend from Digby was the introduction of party politics into this matter. That was not at all necessary and did not add at all to the strength of his argument.
What politics did I introduce?

I refer to my hon.
friend's statement at the outset that it was very necessary to perform a surgical operation on some part or limb of the Marine and Fisheries Department. He almost provoked me into saying that possibly an operation might be beneficial somewhere else just as well. But leaving that point- and I have no other fault to find with the observations of the hon. member-and possibly his introduction of politics to the extent he did was because he may have thought it necessary to stamp himself clearly and distinctly so as to show to which side of the House he belonged, and we know that some of the men in the colony opposite might be charged with supporting the Opposition while they are supporting the Government-let me say that, although I may be called a new member, I was in this House a little while once before, and had then the opportunity of saying something very much along the lines of the remarks made by the hon. gentleman who has moved this resolution (Mr. Sinclair) and I wish to express my endorsation of what he said. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) has given much credit, and with perfect truth, to Mr. Nickerson, member of the local House for the county of Shel-bourne, for what he has done to improve the condition of our fishermen. But let me tell my hon. friend that I was also in the local House at that time and so was my hon. friend who moved this resolution (Mr. Sinclair), and the first time that Mr. Nickerson ever appeared as a member of a committee appointed to deal with fishery matters, was upon a committee moved for
by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). Yet it would almost appear, from [DOT] the remark of the hon. member from Digby that Mr. Nickerson had to fight a battle in the local House in order to get such concessions for the fishermen of Nova Scotia as they were entitled to and in order to bring their case before the public. My experience in the local House does not bear out that contention. I always found that the members of that House were ever willing to do whatever they could in behalf of any industry in the maritime provinces or in any part of Canada which could be benefited by anything our local legislature could do. I would not like to charge any member with a desire to do otherwise than promote to the best of his ability any industry in this country which might tend to the general welfare and add to the comfort and wealth of the people. The consensus of opinion expressed to-day in favour of the resolution before us would bear out that remark. I do not think that we have to expect from either side other than the fullest and best assistance in all such matters. As regards this resolution, it is not necessary that I should say anything in its behalf because there is only one side to it. No one can question that the case is a strong one and that the fishing industry is most important and if the appointment of the committee is going to aid the further development of that industry there can be no possible objection. So far as the county I have the honour to represent is concerned, I may say that we catch more fish on the coast of Victoria county than; possibly in any other county in the Dominion, and we enjoy the reputation of making the best cured fish that can be procured in the maritime provinces. There is a gentleman in Halifax, whose name I do not recall at the moment, who last year was called upon to gather for some people in the United States a large quantity of first-class fish. I am proud to say that he found more of ythe high grade fish he required along the northern part of Victoria county than in any other part of the maritime provinces. I agree with my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) that it is not the Department of Marine and Fisheries alone which can assist in developing this great industry. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his department have done much, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), but the Department of Railways can also come into play in this matter. That department can do a good deal in furnishing the proper kind of cars fitted for this industry, and we look to it to furnish first-class cars and give us such rates as will enable us to place our fish in the markets of central Canada and incidentally in some of the markets further west and also in the United States. The Department of

Public Works can also do much to help out the fishermen, especially along the exposed coast in Nova Scotia, and in that connection our position is perhaps not as well understood by some of our members from the west as it ought to be. We find that our fish are taken away from our very doors by Americans who are better equipped than we are, and with whom we cannot compete successfully on account of our lack of harbour facilities and of large vessels and boats. The consequence is that American schooners come from Boston and other places along the coast right up to the edge of the three-mile limit and sometimes within that limit, and catch our fish and carry it to the United States markets and sell it there whence it often finds its way back to Canada and is sold in Toronto and Montreal and other large centres. That is the condition of things which exist to-day, and it does not require any argument to point out how much better it would be to have our fish caught by our own people, along our coast, and carried directly to, our own markets and sold to our own people. Our fishermen would then get better prices than they can to-day, even when they sell to Americans and our consumers would get fresher fish at less prices. It will therefore be necessary for the Public Works Department to spend some money in giving us harbours of refuge at different places and thus enable our fishermen to compete wdth the Americans who have larger vessels and are in a better condition to catch fish. I cordially endorse what my hon. friend from Richmond has said to the effect that wherever possible we should do something for our fisheries, by lowering the customs duties, particularly upon their nets or engines or whatever else enters into that industry, and in every other possible way. I may say in conclusion that I agree entirely in the observations of the different gentlemen who have addressed the House in this matter. I did not rise for the purpose of making out a case because that was made out by the mover of the resolution, and the case required only to be stated to the House in order to make it clear that whatever we can do to carry forward this great industry should be done by the government with the assistance of every hon. member of this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MADDIN (Cape Breton South).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to take part in this debate and to express my approval of the resolution as moved by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). I agree with some of the speakers who have preceded me that the fishing industry in Nova Scotia has decayed to some extent of late years, and that this is true of the fisheries of the whole Atlantic sea-board of Canada. A number of causes have contributed to the decadence of this industry, most of which have been enumerated by the Mr. McKenzie.
speakers who preceded me. But I would suggest that one reason why the fisheries of Nova Scotia, and the maritime provinces generally, are not prosecuted more closely than they have been of late years i;s to be found in the local conditions obtaining in the fishing villages. The social conditions and environment are so different from those of other parts of the province that there are but slight inducements to the rising generation to remain in these fishing villages. For instance, I would call the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) to the fact that there are a large number of fishing villages on the Atlantic sea-board in which they have only one mail a week. Cut off from railway facilities, from telegraph and telephone lines, these places are so isolated, so cut off from society, that there is but little to attract the rising generation to continue to live in them and prosecute the fisheries. I agree with the speakers who have preceded me on both sides in approving this resolution. I believe a committee such as is proposed, will have a far-reaching effect in restoring conditions in connection with the fisheries of the maritime provinces. And, if the scope of this committee is made wide enough, and its inquiries go far enough, they may develop a number of causes that have led to the conditions now existing and that are not generally known to the members of this House or to the people of this Dominion. It was only a matter of eighteen months ago that I counted 31 American schooners fishing off the coast of my county in broad daylight and well within the three mile limit, and no gunboat there to protect the interests of the people of Nova Scotia. It is pretty well known that a large percentage of the mackerel catch of the Gloucester fleet around our Coast 'are taken within thte three mile limit. And it is well within the knowledge of some members of this House that a vessel loaded to the hatches with mackerel, caught within two miles of the shore was taken to the port of Halifax, and that, after the vessel had lain there two or three weeks, her owners paid $400 and she was released. Our law is clear on this subject. If that vessel was guilty of infringing our law both cargo and vessel should have been seized and confiscated, but if she wa3 not guilty, both should have been released without penalty. There are American capitalists who would readily capitalize companies to-morrow to come within our three-mile limit, deplete our inshore fisheries, and load their vessels to the hatches with mackerel, if they could do. it on paying a fine of $400. Then, if I may, I would bring to the attention of the House the question of license for the packing of fish. In the province of Nova Scotia, I believe, the whole catch of the lobster fishery is packed by ten or twelve concerns. Under the con-

ditions that exist, whilst the fishermen are paid a certain amount per pound live weight, they are not informed with regard to market values of the packed article and so do not know what value to put upon their catch. I am at a loss to know, and should be glad to be informed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or any hon. member of this House, why it is that a man who catches lobsters cannot come ashore and can them as he dries his codfish or pickles his herring or mackerel. Why so important an industry as lobster packing should be a monopoly in the hands of ten or twelve people who are enabled to get a license to pack the catch is a matter wholly beyond me. With regard to the other aspect of the question, the social conditions in the fishing villages, this might be helped by daily mail services, and this is a subject that the Postmaster General might take up in the broad manner which has characterized him in other things. I do not wish to approach this question in a partisan spirit or drag politics in. I well believe that it is the desire of the Postmaster General to facilitate the mail service and to grant services as far as possible. If he would take into consideration the claims of the fishing villages in the isolated parts of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-and perhaps in the province of British Columbia for all I know-it would go a long way to make the homes in these villages more attractive to the young people and so induce them to remain. I strongly endorse this resolution of the hon. member for Guys-borough, believing that it will result in good to those who go down to the sea in ships and brave the perils of the deep, who are such an important class to the Dominion of Canada, and who at great danger to themselves are contributors in no small measure to the wealth of Canada on both the Atlantic and Pacific sea-boards.

LOGGIE (Northumberland, N.B.) It seems to me that we have wandered far over this resolution, and that we have discussed the merits of the fishing industry more than the merits of the resolution itself. I may add, however, that there can be no question that the problem of transportation is so intertwined with that of the fishing industry, that if anything can be done to improve transportation it certainly would be in the interest not only of the producers but of the consumers of fish in Canada. It seems to me that Ontario and Quebec should consume more of our eastern fish than they do. It is to be regretted that fish coming from the American sea-board should be brought in under duty and consumed by the cities of Toronto and Montreal instead of their bringing in fish from Halifax or other sea-board towns in Canada. In my own county, the urgent matter is transportation.
For example, a petition has been presented to the government asking them to build a branch line along the Miramichi river, and along the sea coast, a coast where large quantities of smelts are at present taken and during the summer season large quantities of Atlantic salmon. These fish, during the winter season, have to be teamed about twenty miles to the nearest Intercolonial railway station, and then, if they are to be sent off in a fresh condition, must be sent by express. I want to say that the express rates, although they are lower than in former years, are still too high, and if anything can be done to bring about a reduction in the express charges on fresh fish. I believe it would be in the interest of all concerned, of the consumer as well as of the producer. It seems to me that if the committee suggested in the resolution can assist in any way to bring that about it would certainly do some good. It is really singular that now we seem to be united on the importance of this resolution, and yet parliament has been discussing the management of the Marine and Fisheries more or less for the last forty years without action in this regard. Judging from the expressions we have heard from both sides, we wonder why a committee of this nature was not heretofore appointed. I certainly think it would be in the interest of the country at large that it should be appointed at once.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. DANIEL (St. John City).
speechtext:
I did not anticipate making any remarks on this resolution, but after hearing the statements that have been made by hon. gentle men on both sides, I feel that I cannot allow the opportunity to pass without saying a word or two. I have great pleasure indeed in supporting the resolution which has been brought before the House by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). Although I come from a part of the country where the inhabitants are perhaps not so deeply interested in fishery questions as they are in Nova Scotia, still I can say that the fisheries of the Bay of Fundy are very valuable, and should be preserved and developed. We have there, on both sides of the bay, both on the Nova Scotia side and the New Brunswick side, very valuable fisheries indeed. The regulations that have been framed, I was going to say enforced, but I cannot go that far-the regulations of the Marine Department in regard to bay fishing, and inshore fishing, and river fishing are not carried out. I have heard it stated over and over again that the fishery overseers find it almost useless to prosecute men for breaking the regulations, because as soon as a man is reported, influence is brought to bear in his favour, the fine is remitted, and the fishery officer is discouraged from doing his duty. A great deal of that is done. I

think that, if a special committee such as proposed by this resolution were appointed to look into these matters, and were given some measure of control, the regulations of the department would he better carried out. Several other important matters in connection with the fisheries have been brought up this afternoon. There is the curing of fish, and the packing of fish. I understand from a little booklet that has been distributed among the members that the packing of fish in the maritime provinces is very badly done, that there is no standard package, that the packages leak, and the fish put into them are allowed to deteriorate in quality; the packages are not tight enough and strong enough, and the brime leaks out to the consequent damage of the fish. These are some of the important matters that such a committee might look after. Then there is the matter of dynamiting fish. I saw in the press the other day that some American fishermen were driven off from some of our inland waters for dynamiting fish. I may say, although I have heard it contradicted in this House, that the inland waters of Canada are not the only waters on which dynamiting takes place. I have myself, when sailing on the Bay ofj Fundy, heard shots fired by persons who were dynamiting fish. This is something that ought to be looked into, along with the other matters I have mentioned.
Then there is the matter of the dogfish nuisance which has several times engaged the attention of this House. Last year I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was presented with a petition from the Board of Trade of St. John, who were requested to do so by a large number of fishermen residing on the Bay of Fundy, the petition dealing with the Dogfish Reduction Works. A copy of it was put into my hands, and I took the trouble to communicate with several persons whom I thought would be able to give me some information as to the success or non-success which was attending the establishment of these reduction works. I will ask the House to listen while I read some of the communications I have received. They are from practical men, and would be of value in a consideration of this subject. The first letter I wrote was to A. H. Whitman, of Canso, N.8., whose name I think the minister will remember, andj I am sure the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) is acquainted with it. I asked my correspondents to reply to the following questions:
1.	Are the reduction works an advantage to the fishermen? If so, in what way?
2.	Is the price paid for dogfish fair and reasonable ?
3.	Do the establishment and use of the reduction works have any effect in diminishing the numbers of dogfish?

I will first read Mr. Whitman's letter, which is signed by A. H. Whitman & Son, Ltd.:
Canso, N.S., January 23, 1908.
J. W. Daniel, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-We have yonr favour of 13th instant, and may say in reply that the dogfish reduction works here have not yet reached a point where they can be called a commercial success.
They operated only a few weeks last season while the dogfish were so plentiful as to interfere with the catching of food fish. We were much less troubled with dogfish in 1907, than for several years past, and are of the opinion that they are leaving these shores.
The quality of both fertilizer and oil manufactured each year has improved as the men have become more familiar with the work. The fishermen will not catch dogfish when they can get any other fish to catch. The quantity caught makes so little impression upon the hordes that used to infest the coast that it cannot be noticed.

Goodwin, George Walsb, Jobn McNeary and James Lumsden are four intelligent fishermen here who probably have opinions of their own about this dogfish work. As a rule the fishermen are glad to have it in operation, hut unless dogfish are very plentyful it is operated only at a loss.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that I asked this gentleman to furnish me with the names of some fishermen who would be able to give information as to the success or otherwise of these reduction works. I will read the replies I received from these men, every one a practical fishermen:
Canso, N.S., February 15, 1908.
J. W. Daniel, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of yonr favour inquiring about the dogfish reduction wojks, and in reply beg to say.
This is the question :
1.	Are the reduction works an advantage to the fishermen, if so in what way? Materially in giving employment at the time when no other branch of fishing can be successfully prosecuted on account of the dogfish pest.
2.	Is the price paid for dogfish fair and reasonable? No, I think not, it does not warrant a general outlay for catching them.
3.	Does the establishment and use of the Reduction Works have any effect in diminishing the number of dogfish? I cannot say, there is so few caught that they are not missed much from the great schools that invade our shores. I might say that one of our oldest citizens, who has made a success of fishing, says in his opinion the Reduction Works is the best thing the government has ever done for the fishermen.
Hoping you may use your influence for the establishment of a number more along the coast, I remain, yours very truly, E. M. Goodwin.

The next letter is from James R. Lums-den:
1.	Are the Reduction Works an advantage to the fishermen? If so, in what way? Yes, in the first place when the dogfish come in on the shore it puts a stop to all other fishing as they destroy nets and gear. The fisherman can make very good pay in catching them.
2.	Is the price paid for dogfish fair and reasonable? Yes.
3.	Does the establishment and use of the Reduction Works have any effect in diminishing the numbers of dogfish? I do not think the Reduction works has been in operation long enough to answer that question, but the dogfish in our bay for the year 1907 were the scarcest they have been for years. Whether the Reduction Works had anything to do with it or not or some other cause I don't know. My opinion is that there ought to be several reduction plants along the shore as it is quite a task for one plant to do the work because it cannot grind up all that is caught in this place.
I remain, yours truly, (Sgd.) JAMES R. LUMSDEN,
The next reply is from George Walsh:
Dear Sir,-By the use of the Reduction Works these pests become an industry and are disposed of for value which certainly is an advantage to fishermen.
The price paid for dogfish is fair and reasonable.
Use of the Reduction Works has an effect in diminishing the dogfish.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) GEORGE WALSH.
There is only one more letter and I will read that:
Sir,-In reply to your; respective inquiries re the Reduction Works at Canso, I wish to say they are a great advantage to our fishermen; they afford a market for dogfish which infest our fishing grounds from August until about the end of October and which formerly prevented our men from fishing during those months.
At the price paid for dogfish a man can make a fair day's pay when fish are plentiful.
Dogfish were not nearly so plentiful on our fishing grounds last year as in former years. I believe the numbers of dogfish will decrease in proportion to the number of reduction works in operation.
I am, sir,	, ,
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) JOHN McNEARY, Canso, N.S.
These are the opinions of practical fishermen and each one of them approves of the establishment of dogfish reduction works. As far as the Bay of Fundy is concerned we have no dogfish reduction works there and I know from practical experience, having seen them, that the Bay of Fundy is filled with these pests to the detriment, I was almost going to say, destruction, of the food fish which come
into that bay in such large quantities. They are so destructive that they destroy the nets, they destroy the food 'fish that are on the hooks of the trawls even as they are being hauled from the bottom of the sea up to the boats to be taken in by the fishermen. When I spoke upon this question before I referred to a very graphic description given to me by one of the fishermen whom I interviewed after he had come ashore and who assured me that of a.catch upon the trawls, which contained about 2,000 hooks, 1,700 food fish, as they drew them up to their boats, had been eaten off to the heads by the dogfish and destroyed; so that instead of having a good haul of food fish the man who had spent his time had simply made a haul of heads of food fish and the hooks that were hanging to the trawls. That is something that took place to my own knowledge in the Bay of Fundy and it is a striking example of what is taking place there all the time. I think that matter is one that might well be taken up by a committee such as is foreshadowed by the resolution before the House moved by the hon. member for Guysborough. There are other points which I might bring up but most of them have already been brought before the House by those who have preceded me. I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the House to be allowed to say one word in support of this resolution. There is only one course to be taken by the House and that is the adoption of this resolution. Many things have been said and well said in favour of the resolution. There is no doubt that the trouble with regard to the fishing industry does not lie with the lack of improved apparatus or of facilities for catching fish, but I think that the whole trouble comes from the lack of proper facilities for selling the fishermen's product. As a matter of fact, most of the fish caught along the shores of the maritime provinces are sold in the United States, and the people of Montreal have been in the habit for the last twenty years of importing part of this same fish into Canada. We have been paying for the last ten years as much as $5,000 per week to the railway companies for the transportation of fresh fish from the United States to Montreal. We have been paying to this government as much as $3,000 per week for duty on that fish. I think that the difficulties against which the fishermen of the maritime provinces are now contending arise from the lack of proper facilities, such as refrigerators and fish markets, in the great cities of the central portion of Canada. By establishing a system of fish refrigerators along our coast, by building especially equipped railway cars for the transportation of live fish ac-
