cording to the German fashion, by transporting the fish rapidly from the seashore to the great cities and by the construction of buildings or fish markets in Montreal, Toronto and elsewhere for the proper handling and sale of fish, the existing difficulties will be largely overcome and the fishermen of the maritime provinces will again enjoy that progress and prosperity with which they were blessed in bygone days.

Mr. Speaker, before the minister replies I would like to say a word or two with reference to this question. Those who are older in time and experience in the House I think cannot but feel very great satisfaction in listening to the discussion which has taken place this afternoon. The discussion has not been directed to the end of passing the resolution. That I suppose was a foregone conclusion from the first; the discussion has rather tended towards eliciting information and suggestions from a great many different points of view as to the fishery industry in all its phases. With reference to the resolution itself, I have not heard any good reasons why the two departments of Marine and Fisheries should be included in it. There is a very wide field of work for such a committee with reference to the fisheries, but it seems to me that the department itself ought to be quite capable of dealing with what are peculiarly marine matters. Now, we are going to have this committee and very possibly it is but the forerunner of other such committees. _ We must keep in mind that while economizing the time of parliament we must not by the appointment of committees deprive the House itself of its proper workers. As a rule our committees are too large; they might with a very great deal of profit be very largely diminished in the numbers of their members, because the larger the committee the greater the aggregate of party feeling in it and the more numerous the extraneous questions which are discussed. In my opinion the actual power for work of a committee increases in the ratio of the fewness of its members. We lose a vast deal of time in some of our large committees, and holding this opinion I would not have this committee composed of more than 15 or 20 members, selected from both sides of the House. I would have it an absolutely good working committee, not a committee which would be fishing for this or fishing for that, but a committee which went straight at its object of conserving our fish resources and broadening and developing the industry. If we are to have committees on our great natural resources there will be three or four more of such, and, in my opinion, no man can serve efficiently upon more than two committees. If he does his work well on one important committee, that, _ together with his work on the floor of this House, Mr. GERVAIS.
and the conduct of his correspondence, gives him plenty to do. With reference to the fishery question itself, I think it will be acknowledged by all members of this House that the tendency is, each year that passes, towards the greater depletion of the fisheries. That is the tendency in our lumber industry, it is the tendency in our coal and mineral industries, but it is more particularly the tendency with regard to our fisheries. Our population is continually increasing, fish foods are more eaten, the means of transportation are every day becoming better and cheaper, fresh fish is more easily obtained and there is a greater consumption of it. As the price of fish rises, and it is constantly rising, old methods give place to new; the less destructive methods of catching fish are supplanted by more destructive methods and the constant effort is to take as many of the denizens of the waters as possible from their habitat and transfer them to the tables of the people. All this is a constant menace to our fisheries. There is more than that. Don't let the people of the maritime provinces think that the only fish in the world are to be found in the salt water. The fisheries in our inland waters are of immense benefit to our people. The source of supply from these inland fisheries is near to the people and it is most important that there should be a perennial never failing supply of fish from these inland waters. Both the inland and the salt water fisheries are of course important, but with the distribution of the increased population in our country, the inland fishery industry is perhaps more important still. If, in view of the increasing demand, you allow destructive methods of fishing then the inland fisheries will be depleted in such a ratio that it does not require very long vision to see the practical disappearance of our food fish. To-day the vast majority of fish that are taken from our inland waters are transported to the markets of another country and are eaten by people in Chicago, Detroit, or Boston, who do not care if it is the last fish in the stream so long as they get it on their breakfast table. The Minister of Marine, the members of the government, the members of this House, have read the statistics and they know that this is the truth. It is time there was a stop put to it. It may be ultra doctrine but it is a doctrine that every good Canadian will subscribe to that the food fishes of this country exist primarily for the consumption of the people of Canada, not even for the consumption of this generation of Canadians but for the consumption of future generations. If we set our minds to it, it is possible for us to keep up a perennial supply of fish in these inland waters, as well as in our salt waters, so long as Canadians require fish food. I do not believe that any one will doubt

that. But we have to be more heroic than we have been. The minister has got to be able to say to the supporter who comes to him, when both of them are absolutely certain that all the fish have been taken out in that season that ought to be taken out, that he will not permit any extension of the close season, or any departure from the regulations, that he will not yield to any request or any pressure, however strong. I know as an administrator in that department and as an observant member of the body politic, that this is a tremendous force in this country, and we have got somehow or other to eliminate patronage from the fisheries of this country. That one sentence contains it all. We have got to place this branch of the public service either departmentally or by a commission, under hard and fast, scientific, reasonable, common-sense jurisdiction and administration. If we do that we can have fish, if we do not do that we will come to a time when we will not have fish. I have a letter from a man who knows what fisheries are, because he was born amongst them, brought up with them and spent a part of his life in both fishing and dealing and has taken a wide interest in the subject. What does he tell me ? Within ten years, unless we do something more than we are doing now, it will not be possible to get a decent sized lobster along the Atlantic coast of Canada. We have been warned about that. The lobsters have been a diminishing race until they have almost entirely vanished from the coast of the United States, they have been pushed gradually, further and further north until they have now passed the Maine coast which has a very little remnant of lobster fishing left and the Americans are invading our coast. To-day you boil lobsters from 4 to 9 inches long. The law says you shall not, but the inspector does not say you shall not nor does the administration. This man writes and gives instances where inspectors shut their eyes to the fact that hundreds of thousands of lobsters were boiled last year and canned which were from four to nine inches in length, more nearer four than nine.
Now we must, government and opposition, set our faces like flint with reference to these great fish resources of this country, if we hope to keep them and to hand to our children those inestimable blessings of food fishes which have been ours so luxuriously and abundantly. To-day we have six million people, before long we will have twelve million, then twenty, then thirty, then forty million, and still I say that if we do rightly in this matter our forty million people can have their food fishes many years from now just as we have them now, but they cannot unless we take hold of this matter.
Then we want education. I do not believe that a fisherman, although he is born in the brine and goes to sea every day in 17
the! year, ever passes the time when some good information will not be useful to him. Your farmer is in the same position, so is every man. We do not grow up into special knowledge. What has been done by the Department of Agriculture ? Whatever has not been done or has been done, whatever have been the lapses or excellencies of that department, one thing is certain, that by a persistent method of generally enlightened education they have taught the farmers of this country and have brought them up by large strides ahead of where they were before this education began. I think a similar method of education can be adopted for the fishermen. It is one thing to catch a fish, it is another thing to land that fish on the table of the ultimate consumer, so that the fisherman shall have as large a proportion of the profit as possible, and this cannot be done unless proper methods are used. I am not here to teach the fishermen, I cannot do it, I do not know myself what is necessary, but I say that the Fisheries Department ought to lay itself out to get at methods not so much of catching fish, the fishermen will attend to that, but methods of curing, packing, and all that tends to make the ultimate market value the highest possible and so bring the greatest profit to the person who is engaged in the business. I am heartily in favour of this resolution. I was glad to hear our young men take such sane ground and such intelligent ground with reference to this matter as they have this afternoon. I have seldom heard a debate in this House participated in by so many young men which has been so free from anything that was not germane to the subject and which has been stuffed so full of good common sense, as the speeches we have heard this afternoon from our young members.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we must congratulate ourselves upon the contributions which have been made to this debate by some of the new members of the House. Their knowledge of local circumstances has enabled them to give us the best information upon the important question of the! fisheries. I hope this will not be the last time when this question of fisheries will come before the House and we will hear such! speeches as we have heard to-day. I congratulate the new members very heartily upon the way in which they have discharged their duties in the circumstances, and I am sure that this debate will have a very good effect on the relations between these members and the administration of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Several important questions have been dealt with during this debate. I shall first discuss the question which is at _ issue, namely the formation of a new committee of this House. Committees of this House



are formed for the purpose of dealing with the ordinary legislation or with the work of the session. The session is called for a special purpose, for the purpose of passing laws and making legislation, the voting of supplies and the controlling and investigating of expenditures. Bills which c^me up before this House are generally referred to the committees in order that a few members may devote more time to the questions involved in these Bills than wou'd be possible in the House. It would be, I think, contrary to the ordinary principles which are followed in the British House of Commons if we were to form committees which will make all sorts of investigations. I understand that in some cases investigations are absolutely necessary, but the particular work which the committees are called on to perform is the work of legislation. That is, I am sure, the object which my hon. friend had in view when he proposed that a committee of this House should be appointed to look into the questions relating to Marine and Fisheries. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said a few minutes ago that no reason had been adduced in the debate whv the Marine should be joined with the Fisheries in this committee. During two or three of our last sessions some very important Bills were brought before this House relating to marine. These were referred to special committees whrh investigated and reported, and these reports were embodied in the laws we passed last session. When last year my hon. friend made a motion for the fo-mat;on of a committee on Fisheries, I asked him whether he would not be willing to add to this resolution the subject of Marine, as the two were very closely connected, and might be investigated by the same committee. That was the object I had in view. Various important Bills come up nearly every vear concerning Marine, and I thought that since it was the opinion of the House and the government that we should have a Committee on Fisheries, it would be just as well to give to that committee the power to deal with the questions of Marine. That is why I asked my hon. friend to add to his motion questions affecting Marine as well as i those affecting Fisheries. In England and in the United States it is the same committee which deals with both questions.
I am glad to see that there is no objection at all to the formation of this committee, and the government accepts with the greatest pleasure the motion made by my hon. friend, and in a few days will be able to submit amendments to our existing rules, which no doubt will receive the unanimous consent of the whole House?
My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), has mentioned some of the things which have been done by the government, and has spoken of the importance of improving our transportation system. Several ' Mr. BRODEUR.
other members have also dealt with this question, and I may be permitted to say a word or two on it. I was sorry indeed to find out, when I came to the department, that a large quantity of our fish, instead of being shipped direct from the maritime provinces or the great lakes to our centres of consumption, were sent to the United States and in some cases reshipped from the United States to Canada. It is a great pity indeed that our fisheries should be exploited by American fishermen in this way, and I thought that by encouraging the transportation of fish from the maritime provinces and the great lakes to Canadian centres we would hereby divert that trade from the United States. I was also sorry to hear that some of our banking institutions were not very willing to lend money on our fisheries. I do not know why they refused to give advances for the development of that valuable industry, with the result that the business, instead of being carried on by our own people, was carried on by Americans. I have no objection to our exporting some of our fish, as we are producing much more than we consume- and have to depend on foreign markets to some extent, but I regret, in common with my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that any exporting should be done to our detriment and that our fisheries should become depleted. It therefore becomes necessary to find out whether there be not some means of preventing it. As regards transportation, let me state what we did last year with the $25,000 voted by parliament. During the months of September, October, and November, the department made an arrangement with the Express Companies by which these companies charged the shippers of fish on.'y two-thirds of the regular express rates, and collected the other one-third from the department. This gave the shipper from Halifax to Montreal $1 per 100 lbs. The express rate from Boston to Montreal is 80 cents, and the duty $1, making the total $1.80 per 100 lbs., thus giving an advantage to the shippers from the maritime provinces to Montreal over the shippers to American ports. The result has been extraordinary. It is true that the Minister of Customs received less revenue from fish, evidently as the result of the policv we have pursued. But I have been glad to hear from merchants in Halifax and in Montreal that there is a larger demand for fish brought direct from our Atlantic sea-board. One merchant in Montreal, I am informed, received 50,000 pounds more within one month than he used to receive in former years. This he attributes to the policv we have adopted. The cost to the department is almost nothing. I have not the figures by me at the moment, but they are very small. We intend to continue the policy, and have agreed to renew the arrangement, beginning on the 20th instant.

I do not think it necessary to go at length into a description of what the government has done for the development of the fisheries. I may mention briefly the cold storage for bait and also the cold storage for fish that we have established. Each of these is very important, the latter being the means of putting the fish on the market in the proper condition. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) has referred to the dogfish. The reduction works that we have established are more or less of an experimental nature. I realize that they have not been a commercial success so far. For that reason, we cannot expect private parties to enter upon this industry now. But we are going to carry on these experiments for some time yet, and, should we be able to prove that this work can be carried on on a commercial basis, we expect that private capital will embark in the industry and that there will be no further necessity for the government to carry on these experiments. We have established also hatcheries in different parts of the country, and it is expected that, with the money to be voted for next year, others may be established. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) has spoken of the way in which our statistics are collected, and has given an instance in which figures were collected from the fishermen and afterwards from those in charge of curing establishments and the two were added together in the report. I should be greatly surprised if this could happen. However, if my hon. friend has the exact information at hand, he would oblige me greatly by giving it to me, in order that a recurrence of such instances may be prevented.
I would like to ask the minister if an officer of his own department was not sent to Nova Scotia to inquire into this very matter of discrepancy in these statistics?

If my hon. friend will give me, even privately, the information in regard to the case he speaks of, I will see to it that instructions are given-or repeated, for instructions have already been given -as to the way these statistics should be collected. We have no desire that the results as shown by the figures should be different from what they are in fact. My hon. friend from Digby has spoken of the question of the fishery board. I agree with him; I am not ready to accept the idea of forming a board on the same lines as that which they have in Scotland. I do not think the time has come when such a board can be formed here to advantage. I find that the people in Scotland at the present day do not take advantage of the inspection provided by the board to so great an extent as might be expected. So long as the imperial government gave the money for the brand-171
ing of the herring, the system went on very well, but when the payments ceased and the standard was raised there was a change.
I see that during 1906 out of 1,967,862 barrels of herring sold, only 306,033 barrels were branded under the authority of the Fishery Board. Of course, a tax has to be paid for the branding of that herring, and people there, like people in this country, do not wish to be taxed, and so they are not taking advantage of this system of branding to as great an extent as formerly, owing largely of course to the high general standard of private trade marks.
My hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) says-and the same was said by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster)-that party politics should not interfere with the administration of fisheries. So far as the department is concerned, there is no party politics in the administration of the fisheries. We see to it, as well as we can, that the regulations are observed. Of course, it is not an easy matter to enforce regulations restricting the fisheries; such regulations are usually unpopular. The suggestion made by my hon. friend from North Toronto deserves consideration-that we should carry on an educational campaign to cause the fishermen to see that the enforcement of the regulations and the improvement of the methods of curing and packing would be in their own interest. As to this question of curing and packing, some years ago we engaged the services of Mr. Cowie, an experienced man, to come and teach our people to cure herring as they are cured in Scotland. The teaching given by this gentleman has, I believe, been appreciated, and I do not know of any place where his visits have not been received with delight by the fishermen and also by those engaged in curing and packing the herring.
My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) referred to the very important Question of the modus vivendi. I would not like to discuss that question at length, but, speaking for myself, I think that the modus vivendi is not of so much benefit as some people believe. The result is that when the Americans come into our waters and procure tnis license to enable them to purchase supplies and outfits, to ship crews and to tranship cargoes, they are practically taking the business away from our own fishermen, they are simply controlling the business which should be done by our own fishermen, and any profits or benefit that might accrue in those fisheries go to Americans instead of Canadians. That is the view I take personally of this matter. If this committee were formed, I would like to see it study this question, and I hope that some day it will be put in a position to investigate it. I think it is a most important question. This is a business that we should try to keep in Canadian channels for the bene-

fit of our own people. There is no reason why this business should be controlled by Americans instead of Canadians. We have the resources, we have the money, we have the intelligence among Canadians, and we ought to control the business. That is my personal view of the matter.
My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has alluded to the question of steam trawlers. In some parts of Europe steam trawlers are considered a very desirable method of fishing, but I do not think that so far they have been considered as such in our own country. Even in Europe there is a great divergence of opinion as to whether they should be used or not. In some parts of France, however, steam trawlers are used to a considerable extent, they are sent into the north sea and also to the grand banks. But in some other parts of France, especially in Normandy and Brittany, the people are strongly opposed to the use of steam trawlers. In this country there is only one opinion, and that is that steam trawlers should not be permitted within the three mile limit and the bays. So general is this feeling that we passed lately an order in council prohibiting the use of steam trawlers within such limits. Now, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) stated that some American boats had been fishing within the three mile limit, and that although they had been seized by some of our own boats, they were let off without a penalty.

What I said was that I saw thirty-one vessels fishing within the three mile limit. It was not one of these that was seized, but another vessel was seized, as I was informed by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby), and was taken to Halifax and held there for three weeks, and then released on payment of a fine of $400. But that was not one of the boats I saw.

Mr. Speaker, I thought we were discussing the question of the appointment of a committee. If I had known that this discussion was going to take so wide a range, I would have been glad to discuss some of these outside questions myself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has the floor.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has a right to make a point of order.
I must say that instead of discussing the question of the appointment of a committee we have been wandering over the whole fishery question in this country as it has existed for the last ten years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion has certainly been broad, but I think that it all had relation to the advisability of appointing such a committee as is proposed, and brought forth the reasons therefore, and consequently it was in order.

I understand that we have been allowed to discuss the question of the fisheries generally in order to adduce reasons for the appointment of this committee. My hon. friend from Cape Breton stated a fact to which I wish to call the attention of the House for a moment. He stated that some American boats had been fishing within the three mile limit. I am greatly surprised to hear it, because generally speaking our fishery cruisers on the Atlantic coast are very diligent; their instructions are to follow closely American vessels coming there to fish, and to see that they do not come within the three mile limit. I would be greatly surprised to hear that our cruisers have been found remiss in this matter. The officers of our boats are men of great intelligence and experience, like Captain Knowlton, for instance. I would be surprised to hear that he had allowed an American vessel within the three mile limit. I know that when an infraction of the law does occur they take immediate steps, with the means at their disposal, to ascertain the fact, and if they find that the vessel is fishing within the three mile limit she is immediately seized.

I may say that the vessel I referred to was taken into Halifax and tied up there, and Captain Knowlton let her go. I am not here to discuss that matter now, but I will be glad to do so at any future time.
Will my hon. friend give me the name of the boat in order that I may make some inquiries?
I will do that.

Of course, we must remember that it is sometimes difficult to find out exactly whether these boats are within or without the three mile limit. They are cute, they generally keep on the border line, and when they see one of our cruisers coming they immediately get outside the limit. So it is very difficult to detect them in a violation of the law.

I understood the hon. member for Lunenburg to tell the minister that if a boat is seized and held up she has either got to be confiscated or released. I would like to follow him on that subject, but I will not do so now.
If it turns out that in some cases our officers have been remiss in their duties, I will see that no such thing occurs again.
I did not intimate that anybody had not done his duty.

I will not continue the discussion any longer. But in view of the reasons which have been given to this House in favour of the appointment of a committee, I may say that I concur heartily with the motion, and see no objection to its being adopted. We will see that rules are drafted later on, and will bring them down for adoption by the House.
Motion agreed to.

LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara) moved the third reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Railway Act. [DOT]

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: I would ask my hon. friend to allow this to stand. I want to get something practical out of this legislation on level crossings if I can, and I am referring this Bill to. the Chairman of the Railway Commission. He is in Winnipeg, I am sending all the Bills to him. I am not trying to block the Bill or anything of that kind, but I want to get his expression of opinion on all these things and see if I cannot get something practical out of them.

The Bill is a public Bill and if the matter is delayed and then sent back here from the Senate, probably, it will never be concluded during this session, and this slaughter of the people at the railway crossings will go on as it has gone on notwithstanding the fact that we have tried to stop it for three years. This Bill has been very carefully considered by this .House for three years. It is the product of the combined intelligence of the whole of this House after
five years of discussion. I do not think that the chairman of any railway commission can tell us how to make this law. I have every respect for the Chairman of the Railway Commission as an administrator -that is his business-but I do not agree that the Chairman of the Railway Commission can give us any pointers with regard to this legislation. We as legislators are here to make law for him to carry out It is his business to carry out the law that we make in this parliament. It is the people's business to make laws, and although I have the greatest respect for the Chairman of the Railway Commission and for the present Board of Railway Commissioners, it is not within their province to tell us anything about the kind of law that the people want passed; it is their province to carry out to the full the law that we may make. In view of the fact that this House for three years unanimously adopted this as a proper piece of legislation to relieve this terrible evil existing in the country, the slaughter of helpless men, women and children at all these level crossings, we should not further delay. The House of Commons lias dealt with it, the House has done its duty, three years ago the House of Commons put it up to the Senate to do their duty, it has not yet been attended to by the Senate and I warn the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) that I shall have to blame somebody if this Bill is not read a third time and sent on to the Senate as quickly as possible.

I agree with a great deal of what my hon. friend has said, but we want to have something practical. As he remarked, this Bill has been passed three times by the House of Commons. I am in hopes that we can deal with this question in a way that will bring about the result that my hon. friend has in mind, and that we all have in mind, and that is to get rid as quickly as possible of the dangerous level crossings. I know it is our business to legislate but there is no person so competent to give us advice as to the most practical way to bring about the desired result as the men who are putting the law into force.
They do not know the evil like we do.
My hon. friend will see that the men who have to apply the law will be able to give us a lot of useful information as how best to accomplish the object we have in view.
Then we would have to refer all our Bills to the judges.

There have been a great many Bills in the parliaments of the country that have been referred to judges before

they have been passed so as to get them into the shape in which they will bring about practical results.
I never saw one taken out of the House in this way.
It is taken out of its order.

It is not taken out of the House nor out of its order. I am asking this House to let the Bill stand as hundreds stand, and I am giving a reason in support of that request that will appeal to the country. It is that I may have an opportunity of conferring with the Chief of the Board of Railway Commissioners, not to defeat the object of this Bill, but to bring about the practical results that we are all looking for; that is to do away with the dangerous level crossing.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals that there has been the opportunity of a year at least to obtain the opinion of the Chairman of the Railway Commission upon this Bill. It has passed the House at least on two occasions, passed the House unanimously, and it has gone to the Senate by a unanimous vote. It seems to me rather late in the day, after the Bill has been before parliament for so long and there has been so abundant an opportunity to obtain the views of the Chairman of the Railway Commission upon it, to suggest a postponement on that account. I have every possible respect for the opinion of the Chairman of the Railway Commission in this connection, but if he desires any modification, if he suggests any modification and if that modification commends itself to the government it can be presented to the Senate and it can come back to this House for consideration later on. It does not seem to me that the suggestion of the minister is based upon any reasonable consideration for the reasons that he mentioned. In the first place, there has been abundant opportunity for more than a year to obtain the views of the Chairman of the Railway Commission. If that has not been done, it has been due to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals having too much on his mind- I suppose too much work. Well, that is not a good reason for asking delay now. Send the Bill up to the Senate and the views of the Chairman of the Railway Commission can be obtained and acted upon by the government if the government think it advisable that there should be any modification of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the coun-Mr. GRAHAM.
ty of Frontenac which I have the honour to represent has on different occasions seen fit to petition this House, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council and at the present time the Board of Railway Commissioners, that action should be taken for the better protection of the public at level crossings I feel that I should say a word why I think this Bill of my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) should receive its third reading at the present time. I am led to think that there is some reason for this delay other than that which has been advanced by the Minister of Railways. He tells us he wants to consult with the Board of Railway Commissioners, but in view of the fact that at the last election word was sent out by the Grand Trunk Company to its employees in the county of Frontenac to cast their votes against me and in favour of my opponent, I am led to wonder if there is not another reason than that ostensibly given by the Minister of Railways. On three occasions has the House of Commons given expression to its opinion with regard to level crossings, and I was in hopes that to-night that expression of opinion would be repeated by a unanimous assent to the third reading of this Bill. The toll of death at these level crossings throughout the county of Frontenac is ever increasing. In a distance of some seven miles from the village of Collins Bay up to the Grand Trunk crossing at the outer station where two lives were lost on the 26th inst., there have been some fourteen or fifteen lives sacrificed. The rails of the Grand Trunk are red with the blood of victims along that piece of track. How much longer is the sacrifice to continue; how much longer are we going to withhold an emphatic expression of opinion that an end must be put to this state of things. There is no difference of opinion in my county about immediate action being necessary. The people are not only unanimous that action should be taken but they are indignant that action has not been taken sooner. I believe that the railway commissioners are desirous of protecting life and I know they are doing good work, but they are doing that work independently of this parliament. Why should the House delay action now? Will not delay at this time encourage the Senate to repeat its former treatment of the measure? If this were the first time such a measure as this were presented to the House there might be a reason for delay, but this Bill having been passed on several previous occasions there is no necessity for delaying it now, and I voice the opinion of my constituents when I demand that it shall receive its third reading to-day.

We have had this Bill before the House until it has been termed a hardy

annual. We have had it up for five sessions; it has been before special committees ; it has been before general committees; it has been thrice passed upon by the House; we have enunciated as a House of Commons our policy upon the Bill and that policy has been frustrated by the Senate. Although I have great respect for the railway board, I do not think this parliament should surrender its judgment entirely to it. I was anxious the other day that we should have the opinion of the railway board upon the broad question of railway crossings from one end of Canada to the other, as transmitted to the minister. The very first day parliament met I put a series of resolutions on the Order Paper with reference to that matter, but this is a specific question which the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) has advanced persistently from year to year and upon which we have proclaimed the policy of this House of Commons to the country. And because the Senate, for good reasons or otherwise-I am inclined very decidedly to think otherwise-has seen fit to bowl out this Bill there is no reason why we should delay it now unless the Minister of Railways can advance substantial reasons for a change of policy. I trust before this session ends the House shall fully consider the whole question of railway crossings throughout Canada, but that is another question altogether and it affords no^ reason why the special provisions of this Bill should not pass.
I am puzzled at the attitude of the Minister of Railways who thinks it desirable we should have the opinion of the railway board, and yet when the policy of the railway board on the general question of level crossings was transmitted to the Minister of Railways the other day he did not think it well that it should be submitted to the House. No doubt the Minister of Railways had good reasons for withholding that information which was so much desired by this House and so earnestly desired by the people of Canada, but is it logical that he should now recommend delay until he consults the railway board when he has in his possession the opinion of the railway board on a cognate question and refuses to submit it to parliament. The government has had ample time within the last year to consider the attitude of the Senate; they have had ample time to submit this question to the railway board, but in the meantime the sacrifice of life has been increasing and the conditions call for the immediate passage of this Bill. As has been said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), when it is considered by the Senate any reasons that are proper to be submitted to them, by the railway board or otherwise, can be submitted by the ministers for consideration of the Senate and they can send it back for our consideration. In this way proper time will be given for the proper reconsideration of this Bill which was not passed and could not be passed last session by reason of the delay in forwarding the Bill. I have a great desire that in this session we shall have a consideration of the broad question of railway protection throughout Canada, but that is no reason for delaying the passage of this Bill which we have already
considered.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer to this House a few remarks in French, i do not intend to make a speech, but I only wish to ask the hon. Minister of Railways a question. It seems evident that the conditions require the immediate passage of this Bill, and still the hon. gentleman recommends delay until he consults the Railway Board. Should the Board of Railway Commissioners express the opinion that it is not desirable to pass such a law, are we to bow to their decision? Not by any means, that is no reason for delaying the third reading of this Bill. I wait the answer of the Minister of Railways.

It is not a question at all of putting their jurisdiction against ours but we have been dealing with this for two or three years and I am anxious to have a practical result from it in a broad way. I have had a good deal of discussion with the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners upon this question, and I have asked him to put his views on the matter m a concrete form in the way of a Bill and let me read it in that form. My request is a very reasonable one; I would like to have the chairman consider this and give his ideas in concrete form. The Bill submitted by him might not be what we want, but it will be a great help. This is far bevond a private question, it affects the lives of the people. I have a message from the chairman of the Commission saying that he will do this and give me something tangible in a few days.

I suppose the Minister is anxious to stop this continuous killing of people in this country. How will sending this Bill to the Senate in the usual way prevent what he wants to do? The people are demanding protection in this matter. There has been no suggestion in committee or on the second reading of any change in the Bill, and why should it not go to the Senate in the usual way? Every man's constituents from Halifax to Vancouver are demanding the stooping of this toll on human life, and unless something is done the people will take the matter in their own hands. Trains will be derailed, although I do not recommend such a course, if they are going to run at 60 miles an hour through thickly peopled portions

of the community without thought of what occurs to the people on the highways. The people will not stand for all this nonsense. Let us get the opinion of the Chairman of the Railway Commission, and of everybody else that will help us, but let us not delay sending the Bill to the Senate. If the rail-railways want to maintain the speed of their trains, we want speed to counteract the result of that speed. I cannot see why an extraordinary and unusual course should be taken in regard to this'Bill. The minister does not pretend that the Bill would not be good law or wise legislation.
My request is very reasonable. My hon. friend will see that the delay I am asking him for does not interfere with the passage of his Bill, as the Senate have adjourned until the 25th.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is within his rights, and if he wants to press his Bill he can do so, and nobody will object. I call his attention simply to this: he has this legislation very much at heart, and in this he has the sympathy of every man in this country I am sure. What we have seen recently is simply appalling, and a stop not only should, but must, be put to it. I would ask him, however, if he is following the better course to reach the end he has in view, in which we are all prepared to second him. The legislation which he has promised is very drastic. It has twice passed this House unanimously, but it has met with a different fate in the other chamber. The only reason why it was not passed by the Senate is evidently its very drastic character. The moment this Bill passes, every railway company is liable to very heavy penalties. My hon. friend will agree that while it is reasonable that the railway company should be compelled to slacken the speed of trains when passing through thickly settled portions of the community or should take extra precautions if they want to maintain their speed, there are quite a number of localities where a level crossing is not likely to produce very severe danger.
This is limited to congested portions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Exactly, but even so a question arises as to what is a congested part, and further there are many congested parts, and if the companies may be unable, with all the good will they might have-and I do not think they have very much good will in this matter-to at once comply with the requirements of this law, they would be subject to these penalties. The Minister of Railways has already taken up the question with the man who, above all others, is competent to advise in this matter, that is the Chairman of the Railway Board. They have been in conference upon it, and my hon. friend expects that he will Mr. LANCASTER.
have before many days an answer to the inquiries that he has put to the Chairman of the Railway Board, advising him as to what in his judgment would be the best legislation.
The matter has been taken up in other countries. I understand that the state of New York has a Bill similar to the Bill of my hon. friend in intent but not in enactment whereby it is contemplated and enacted that the Bill shall come gradually into force, and perhaps it may be advisable to adopt a similar course here. My hon. friend loses nothing by this delay, but if he wants to go on he is within his right and I shall not interfere. Let me suggest to him that the Bill comes to-morrow as the first order of the day. If it is not dealt with to-morrow it comes up on the following Thursday as the first order.
Will that be the result?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly. I have no intention to take away the right of my hon. friend. This Bill will come up to-morrow. If it should not, it becomes the first order of the day on the following Thursday. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Foster) set down the important motion he had for to-morrow, but he and I forgot that on Thursdays public Bills take precedence of notices of motion, and therefore we shall have to select another day. He will have an opportunity to-morrow or the following Thursday to go on with his motion.

I hope the Prime Minister does not think that my sincerity will entirely run away with my judgment. I see the wisdom of what he points out and I want to hold the friendship of the House with regard to this Bill. I do not want to antagonize people in this House or outside, but I want to prevent this terrible toll if possible. On the understanding which my right hon. friend gives that this Bill will take the head of public Bills and orders, I am content, and I assume that the Minister of Railways will accept his suggestion and accelerate it as much as he can.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.

Thursday, February 4, 1909.
